Kennedy’s New Frontier and the Cold War

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 1: Assess President John F. Kennedy's efforts to contain communism abroad and address civil rights and other social programs at home.

IN MY WORDS: Name one Cold War crisis Kennedy faced. Then tell how well he did with laws at home.

Reading AThe New Frontier at Home

In his speech accepting the 1960 Democratic presidential nomination, John F. Kennedy showcased the muscular language that would characterize his campaign and his presidency: “We stand today on the edge of a New Frontier—the frontier of unknown opportunities and perils—a frontier of unfulfilled hopes and threats.”

President Kennedy had a difficult time launching his New Frontier domestic program, in part because he was not skilled at pushing legislation through Congress. Conservative southern Democrats joined Republicans in blocking the president’s efforts to increase federal aid to education, provide medical insurance for the aged, and establish a cabinet-level department of urban affairs and housing to address inner-city poverty.

Word help: perils = dangers · legislation = laws · conservative = wanting to keep things as they are · urban = city · cabinet-level department = a major part of the government

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “The New Frontier” (p. 1206). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “The New Frontier” (A Contrary Congress) (p. 1209).

Reading BThe Bay of Pigs (1961) and the Berlin Wall

The ragtag group of 1,543 Cuban exiles, trained by the CIA, landed before dawn at the Bay of Pigs on Cuba’s south shore on April 17, 1961. Having been tipped off by spies, Castro had 20,000 soldiers waiting. When Kennedy realized the operation was failing, he refused pleas from the trapped rebels for support from U.S. warplanes. . . . The failed operation humiliated Kennedy and elevated Castro in the eyes of the world.

The Soviets responded on August 13, 1961. They first stopped all traffic between East and West Berlin. Then they began erecting the twenty-seven-mile-long Berlin Wall to prevent thousands of refugees from fleeing communism each week by crossing into West Berlin. . . . As Kennedy said, “Freedom has many difficulties, and democracy is not perfect, but we have never had to put up a wall to keep our people in.”

Word help: CIA = the U.S. spy agency · Castro = Fidel Castro, Cuba’s Communist leader · exiles = people forced to live outside their country · humiliated = embarrassed · refugees = people fleeing danger

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “The New Frontier” (Catastrophe in Cuba; The Vienna Summit Meeting) (p. 1210–1211).

Reading CThe Cuban Missile Crisis (1962)

On October 16, 1962, Kennedy learned that photos taken by U.S. spy planes showed some forty Soviet missile sites and twenty-five jet bombers in Cuba. He and his aides viewed the missiles and their nuclear warheads as an intolerable threat.

On October 22, Kennedy delivered a televised speech of the “highest national urgency.” He coolly announced that the U.S. Navy was establishing a “quarantine” of Cuba to prevent Soviet ships from delivering more weapons, adding that he had “directed the armed forces to prepare for any eventuality.”

In the end, the Soviets agreed to remove the missiles in Cuba in return for a public pledge by the United States never to invade Cuba—and a secret agreement to remove the fifteen U.S. missiles with nuclear warheads from Turkey, near the southern Soviet border.

Word help: intolerable = too dangerous to accept · warheads = the explosive tips of missiles · quarantine = a blockade to stop ships · eventuality = anything that might happen · pledge = promise

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “The New Frontier” (The Cuban Missile Crisis) (p. 1213–1214).

Part 2 of 7

Sit-Ins, Freedom Rides, and Birmingham

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 2: Describe the strategies and achievements of the civil rights movement in the 1960s. Explain the divisions that emerged among its activists and how their successes and failures contributed to the rise of the Black Power movement.

IN MY WORDS: Name two strategies civil rights activists used in the early 1960s. What did they want to happen?

Reading DSit-Ins and SNCC (1960)

The civil rights movement entered a new stage when four African American freshmen from North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College tried to order coffee and doughnuts at an “all-White” Woolworth’s lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, on February 1, 1960.

The “sit-in” did not fail, however. It helped turn civil rights into the nation’s most pressing domestic concern.

In April 1960, some 200 student activists, Black and White, converged in Raleigh, North Carolina, to form the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC—pronounced “snick”). Their goal of what they came to call “the movement” was to intensify the effort to dismantle segregation.

Word help: freshmen = first-year college students · sit-in = a protest where people sit and refuse to leave · domestic = inside the country · converged = came together · dismantle = take apart

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “Expansion of the Civil Rights Movement” (Sit-Ins) (p. 1219).

Reading EThe Freedom Riders (1961)

On May 4, the New York–based Congress of Racial Equality (CORE), led by James Farmer, decided to put “the civil rights movement on wheels” when a courageous group of thirteen Black and White men and women called Freedom Riders boarded two buses traveling from Washington, D.C., through the Lower South to New Orleans.

The Freedom Riders wanted to test a recent federal court ruling that banned racial segregation on buses and trains, and in terminals. They knew there would be confrontations and probably violence. Many of them hastily wrote wills before boarding the buses. “We felt we could count on the racists of the South to create a crisis,” Farmer recalled, “so that the federal government would be compelled to enforce the law.”

Word help: CORE = a civil rights group · terminals = bus and train stations · confrontations = angry face-to-face fights · compelled = forced · enforce = make people obey

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “Expansion of the Civil Rights Movement” (Freedom Rides) (p. 1220).

Reading FBirmingham and the “Letter from Birmingham Jail” (1963)

As thousands marched through the streets on May 7, the all-White police force led by “Bull” Connor used snarling dogs, tear gas, electric cattle prods, and high-pressure fire hoses on the protesters.

More than 3,000 demonstrators were arrested, including King and several White ministers. In his cell, King wrote a “Letter from Birmingham Jail,” a stirring defense of nonviolent civil disobedience that has become a classic document of the civil rights movement. “We know from painful experience,” he stressed, “that freedom is never voluntarily given by the oppressor; it must be demanded by the oppressed.” Still, he refused to condone violence. “One who breaks an unjust law,” King asserted, “must do so openly, lovingly, and with a willingness to accept the penalty.”

King’s efforts prevailed when Birmingham officials finally agreed to end their segregationist practices.

Word help: Bull Connor = Birmingham’s police chief · cattle prods = electric sticks used on cows · nonviolent civil disobedience = peacefully breaking unfair laws and accepting the punishment · oppressor = someone who treats others cruelly · condone = accept

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “Expansion of the Civil Rights Movement” (Birmingham) (p. 1223–1224).

Picture 1Bull Connor’s Dogs, Birmingham, 1963

Norton’s caption: “Chief Eugene ‘Bull’ Connor ordered Birmingham, Alabama, police to unleash their dogs on civil rights demonstrators in May 1963.” (It is a primary source.)

What to look for: the young man = a civil rights demonstrator · the officers = Birmingham police · the dogs = police dogs on leashes · the crowd = people watching

Norton, Ch. 27, “Expansion of the Civil Rights Movement” (Birmingham), photo “Bull Connor’s Dogs” (p. 1223). Primary source.

Part 3 of 7

“I Have a Dream” and Black Power

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 2: Describe the strategies and achievements of the civil rights movement in the 1960s. Explain the divisions that emerged among its activists and how their successes and failures contributed to the rise of the Black Power movement.

IN MY WORDS: How were the ideas of King and the Black Power movement different?

Reading GThe March on Washington (1963)

On August 28, some 250,000 Blacks and Whites, a number of them schoolchildren brought on buses, marched arm in arm down the Mall in Washington, D.C., chanting “Equality now!” and singing “We Shall Overcome.”

The March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom was one of the most influential political demonstrations in American history.

It is a dream deeply rooted in the American dream. I have a dream that one day this nation will rise up and live out the true meaning of its creed: “We hold these truths to be self-evident; that all men are created equal.” I have a dream that one day . . . the sons of former slaves and the sons of former slaveowners will be able to sit together at the table of brotherhood.

Word help: influential = having a big effect · the Mall = the big park in the center of Washington, D.C. · creed = a set of beliefs · self-evident = clearly true · brotherhood = friendship among all people

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “Expansion of the Civil Rights Movement” (“I Have a Dream”) (p. 1225).

Reading HThe Rise of Black Power

White racism was not limited to the South. By the mid-1960s, about 70 percent of the nation’s African Americans were living in blighted urban areas. Many struggled to find jobs and decent housing, and most of them experienced humiliations from racist White policemen. Young Blacks questioned how nonviolent protest could bring any positive changes to their lives.

Urban disorders revealed the growing divide within the civil rights movement. . . . What came to be called “Black power” emerged as the alternative to the integrationist, nonviolent philosophy espoused by Martin Luther King and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference.

Malcolm X expressed the emotions and frustrations of the inner-city African American working poor.

Word help: blighted = run-down and poor · urban disorders = riots in cities · alternative = a different choice · integrationist = wanting races to live together · espoused = supported

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “Expansion of the Civil Rights Movement” (Black Power; Malcolm X and Black Power) (p. 1230–1231).

Part 4 of 7

Johnson’s Great Society

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 3: Analyze Lyndon B. Johnson's War on Poverty and other Great Society initiatives and evaluate their impact on American society.

IN MY WORDS: What was the Great Society trying to fix? Name two laws that were part of it.

Reading ICivil Rights and the War on Poverty (1964)

Long thwarted by southern Democrats in Congress, the Civil Rights Act of 1964 finally became law on July 2. It guaranteed equal treatment for all Americans and outlawed discrimination in public places—theaters, restaurants, parks, hotels, sports arenas, libraries, museums, playgrounds, and other venues—on the basis of race, sex, or national origin.

Lyndon Johnson did not stop with civil rights. He launched an elaborate legislative program that declared “unconditional war on poverty in America.”

The Economic Opportunity Act of 1964 was the primary weapon in Johnson’s War on Poverty. It created an Office of Economic Opportunity (OEO) to administer eleven new community-based programs, many of which still exist.

Word help: thwarted = blocked · discrimination = unfair treatment because of who you are · venues = places · administer = run · community-based = run in local neighborhoods

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “Lyndon Baines Johnson and the Great Society” (The Civil Rights Act (1964); War on Poverty; Economic Opportunity Act of 1964) (p. 1235–1236).

Reading JMedicare and Medicaid, and a New Immigration Law (1965)

Now that Johnson and the Democrats had the votes, however, the AMA joined Republicans in limiting the bill to serve only those over age sixty-five, which came to be called Medicare. Johnson also created a program of federal grants to states to help cover medical expenses for the poor of all ages, known as Medicaid.

Of all the Great Society legislation, one of the most historically significant accomplishments was the Immigration and Nationality Services Act of 1965 (also called the Hart-Celler Act), which President Johnson signed in a ceremony at the base of the Statue of Liberty. . . . The old system, dating to 1924, favored immigrants from western and northern Europe over those from southern and eastern Europe, Asia, and Africa. The new law ended national-origins quotas

Word help: AMA = the American Medical Association, a group of doctors · federal grants = money from the national government · quotas = limits on how many can come from each country · favored = treated better

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “Lyndon Baines Johnson and the Great Society” (The Great Society; Health Insurance, Housing, and Higher Education; The Immigration Act (1965)) (p. 1238–1239).

Reading KThe Voting Rights Act (1965)

The resulting Voting Rights Act of 1965 ensured all citizens the right to vote and authorized the attorney general to send federal officials to register voters in areas that had long experienced racial discrimination. The act banned the various methods, such as requiring literacy tests, which local officials had used to keep Black and Latino citizens from voting.

By the 1970s, Deep South states that had most viciously fought civil rights changes would lead the nation in the number of Black elected officials.

Word help: ensured = made sure · attorney general = the nation’s top law officer · register = sign up · literacy tests = reading tests used to stop people from voting

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “Lyndon Baines Johnson and the Great Society” (Voting Rights Legislation) (p. 1241).

Source 1Johnson’s “Great Society” Speech, 1964 (Primary Source)

In May 1964, President Lyndon Johnson spoke to graduating students at the University of Michigan. In this speech he described his vision for the United States.

“The Great Society rests on abundance and liberty for all. It demands an end to poverty and racial injustice, to which we are totally committed in our time. But that is just the beginning. . . . The Great Society is a place where every child can find knowledge to enrich his mind and to enlarge his talents. . . . But most of all, the Great Society is not a safe harbor, a resting place, a final objective, a finished work. It is a challenge constantly renewed, beckoning us toward a destiny where the meaning of our lives matches the marvelous products of our labor.”

Word help: abundance = having plenty · racial injustice = unfair treatment because of race · enrich = make richer or better · beckoning = calling · destiny = future

Lyndon B. Johnson, speech at the University of Michigan, May 1964. In Norton, Ch. 27, “The Tragedy of Vietnam,” Comparing Perspectives: “Ambitions and Agonies in the 1960s” (p. 1248).

Source 1. According to Johnson, what two problems must the Great Society end? Why does he say it is “just the beginning”?

Purpose. Johnson gave this speech to college graduates. Why would a president describe a big, hopeful goal like this to young people?

Reading LDid the Great Society Work?

The Great Society and War on Poverty did not end urban blight or rural poverty or stubborn social problems, partly because the Vietnam War soon took priority and siphoned away funding, and partly because Johnson’s rhetoric always outpaced the realities of what was possible for government to achieve.

Yet the Great Society did include several lasting triumphs for low-income Americans. Infant mortality has dropped, college completion rates have soared, malnutrition is significantly lower, and far fewer elderly Americans are living below the poverty line and without access to health care.

Word help: urban blight = run-down city areas · siphoned away = drained · rhetoric = speeches and promises · triumphs = big successes · infant mortality = babies dying

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “Lyndon Baines Johnson and the Great Society” (Assessing the Great Society) (p. 1242).

Your judgment. Use Reading L. Give one way the Great Society fell short and one lasting success.

Part 5 of 7

Deeper into Vietnam

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 4: Explain the motivations of Presidents Kennedy and Johnson for deepening military involvement in the Vietnam War.

IN MY WORDS: Why did Kennedy and Johnson send more and more Americans to Vietnam?

Reading MAfraid to “Lose” Vietnam

Initially, Kennedy sent more weapons, money, and some 16,000 military “advisers” (so called to avoid the impression that U.S. soldiers were doing the fighting) to South Vietnam to help shore up Diem’s government. “If I tried to pull out,” Kennedy explained, “we would have another Joe McCarthy red scare on our hands.”

Yet Johnson’s fear of appearing weak in the face of communism outweighed his misgivings. He was convinced that the “loss” of South Vietnam to communism would “shatter my presidency.” As a result, by the end of 1965, there were 184,000 U.S. troops in Vietnam; in 1966, there were 385,000; and by 1969, at the height of the American war effort, 542,000.

Word help: advisers = soldiers sent to train and help, not officially to fight · shore up = make stronger · misgivings = doubts · shatter = break apart

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “The New Frontier” (Kennedy and Vietnam) (p. 1215). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “The Tragedy of Vietnam” (p. 1243).

Reading NThe Tonkin Gulf Resolution (1964)

The official justification for the military escalation—a Defense Department term—was the Tonkin Gulf Resolution, passed by the Senate on August 7, 1964.

On that day, President Johnson told a national television audience that on August 2 and 4, North Vietnamese torpedo boats had attacked two American warships, the U.S.S. Maddox and the U.S.S. C. Turner Joy, in the Gulf of Tonkin, off the coast of North Vietnam. . . . Johnson’s statement was later shown to be false and misleading, because the U.S. ships had actually fired first.

But the facts didn’t matter. Congress had given the president what he wanted, a “blank check” to wage war without officially declaring war. The Tonkin Gulf Resolution empowered Johnson to “take all necessary measures” to protect U.S. forces and “prevent further aggression.”

Word help: escalation = making a war bigger · justification = reason given · torpedo boats = small fast warships · misleading = giving a false idea · blank check = permission to do whatever you want

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “The Tragedy of Vietnam” (Escalation in Vietnam) (p. 1243–1244).

Reading O“A Promise to Keep”

President Johnson’s decision to “Americanize” the war flowed directly from the mistaken assumptions that had long guided U.S. foreign policy during the Cold War. The commitment to contain the spread of communism everywhere around the globe guided Johnson, just as it had his predecessors. “Why are we in Vietnam?” the president asked during a speech in 1965. “We are there because we have a promise to keep. . . . To leave Vietnam to its fate would shake the confidence of all these people in the value of American commitment.”

Word help: Americanize = make it an American war · assumptions = beliefs taken for granted · contain = keep from spreading · predecessors = the presidents before him · commitment = promise

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “The Tragedy of Vietnam” (The Stakes of War) (p. 1245).

The Tonkin Gulf. Use Reading N. What did the Tonkin Gulf Resolution let Johnson do? What was wrong with the story he told the nation?

Part 6 of 7

1968: A Year of Turmoil

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 5: Highlight the issues that propelled Richard Nixon to victory in the 1968 presidential election.

IN MY WORDS: Name two events from 1968 that made Americans want change. Who won the election?

Reading PThe Tet Offensive and Johnson Steps Aside

On January 31, 1968, the first day of the Vietnamese New Year (Tet), some 70,000 Viet Cong and North Vietnamese troops unleashed surprise attacks on U.S. and South Vietnamese forces throughout South Vietnam. Within a few days, American firepower turned the tables and General William Westmoreland, commander of U.S. forces in Vietnam, proclaimed the Tet offensive a major defeat for the Viet Cong, and it was. Yet its political impact in the United States was devastating.

On March 31, 1968, Johnson appeared on national television to announce a limited halt to the bombing of North Vietnam to negotiate a possible cease-fire agreement with the Communists. He closed with an added announcement that shocked the political world: “I shall not seek, and I will not accept, the nomination of my party for another term as your President.”

Word help: Viet Cong = Communist fighters in South Vietnam · offensive = a big attack · devastating = very harmful · nomination = being chosen as a party’s candidate

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “The Tragedy of Vietnam” (The Tet Offensive) (p. 1246–1247). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “The Tragedy of Vietnam” (p. 1250).

Reading QKing’s Murder and the Chicago Convention

King’s murder stunned the world. Riots erupted in more than 100 cities. Forty-six people were killed, all but five of them African Americans.

In August 1968, the nation’s social unrest came to a head at the Chicago Democratic National Convention, where delegates gathered to nominate Lyndon Johnson’s faithful vice president, Hubert H. Humphrey, as the party’s candidate for president. . . . On August 28, outside the convention hall, almost 20,000 police officers and National Guardsmen confronted thousands of anti-war protesters. . . . It was as if the police were the rioters.

Word help: stunned = shocked · convention = a meeting to choose a party’s candidate · National Guardsmen = state soldiers · anti-war = against the Vietnam War

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “The Turmoil of the 1960s” (1968: A Traumatic Year; Chicago and Miami) (p. 1251–1252).

Reading RNixon and the “Silent Majority”

Nixon appealed to what he called the “silent majority” of working- and middle-class Americans, who viewed the “rabble-rousing” street protesters with contempt.

On November 5, 1968, Richard Nixon and Governor Spiro Agnew of Maryland, his running mate, eked out a narrow victory of some 500,000 votes, a margin of about 1 percentage point. The electoral vote was more decisive: 301 for Nixon and 191 for Hubert Humphrey.

Embedded in the election returns was a sobering development for Democrats. Although Democrats did retain majority control in both the House and the Senate, White wage workers—the backbone of the party—were shifting to the Republicans.

Word help: silent majority = ordinary Americans who did not protest · rabble-rousing = stirring up crowds · contempt = strong dislike · eked out = barely won · backbone = main support

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 27, “The Turmoil of the 1960s” (Chicago and Miami; Richard Nixon Triumphant) (p. 1253).

Nixon’s appeal. Use Reading R. Who was the “silent majority”? Why would Nixon’s message appeal to them after the events in Reading Q?
